blocks.text: A clinic in Kano treats a child with pneumonia, but the antibiotic that worked last year no longer clears the infection. The bacteria were not taught to resist the drug; a few already carried a mutation, they survived the treatment, and they passed that trait on. That is natural selection happening in a hospital ward — the same process Darwin used to explain how species change.

blocks.markdown:
## Lamarck's theory — and why it was rejected

Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1809) offered two ideas:

1. **Use and disuse.** Organs that are used become stronger and larger; organs that are not used waste away. A blacksmith's arm thickens; a cave fish loses its eyes.
2. **Inheritance of acquired characters.** Those changes, gained during an individual's life, are passed to the offspring. A giraffe stretching for leaves, generation after generation, would beget longer-necked young.

The theory was rejected because acquired characters do not alter the genes in the gametes. **Weismann** cut the tails off mice for many generations; every litter was still born with tails. A footballer's trained muscles are not inherited by his children. Stretching a neck does not rewrite the DNA that the next generation receives.

blocks.title: Natural selection
blocks.text: The process by which individuals with inherited variations that better fit them to the current environment survive and reproduce more successfully than others, so those advantageous alleles become commoner in the population. The environment does the selecting; humans do not choose (that would be artificial selection).

items: Variation: members of a species already differ (size, colour, enzyme shape, resistance). The variation is genetic, arising by mutation and, in sexual species, by recombination.
Overproduction: more offspring are born than the environment can support.
Struggle for existence: they compete for food, light, water, mates and space, and they face predators and disease.

Survival of the fittest: individuals whose variations give an advantage in that struggle live longer and leave more offspring. 'Fittest' means best suited to the conditions, not necessarily strongest.
Inheritance: the advantageous alleles are passed on. Over many generations the population changes, and given isolation it may become a new species.

blocks.markdown:
## Applying the theory

**Peppered moth.** In unpolluted woodland the pale speckled form is camouflaged on lichen-covered bark and the dark (melanic) form is eaten. After industrial soot darkened the trees, the dark form survived better and became common; when air cleaned up, the pale form increased again. The moths did not choose a colour; selection by birds changed the proportions.

**Antibiotic resistance.** A random mutation (or a plasmid) gives a bacterium an enzyme that destroys the drug. In a patient taking antibiotics, sensitive cells die and resistant cells multiply. Completing a full course, and not using antibiotics for viral colds, reduces that selection pressure.

**Sickle cell and malaria (balanced briefly).** In malarial parts of West Africa the AS heterozygote resists malaria better than AA, while SS suffers sickle cell anaemia. Both homozygotes are at a disadvantage, so natural selection keeps the S allele in the population — a balance, not a march to one extreme.

blocks.title: Explaining antibiotic resistance with Darwin's steps
blocks.prompt: A hospital ward finds that Staphylococcus from wounds no longer dies when penicillin is given. Using Darwin's theory step by step, explain how the resistant population arose. Why is Lamarck's explanation not accepted?

steps.text: Variation: among the bacteria, a few already had a mutation (or a plasmid gene) that made an enzyme able to break down penicillin. They did not acquire it by 'practising' against the drug.
Overproduction and struggle: bacteria multiply rapidly; penicillin is a new, severe environmental pressure.
Survival of the fittest: sensitive cells die; resistant cells survive and divide.
Inheritance: the resistance gene is copied into every daughter cell (and can even move between bacteria on plasmids), so the ward population becomes mostly resistant.

Lamarck would have said the bacteria 'got used' to penicillin and passed that habit on. That fails because exposure does not rewrite DNA in a directed way; only cells that already had the gene survive.

blocks.answer: Pre-existing resistant variants survive penicillin, reproduce, and make resistance common. Lamarck is rejected because acquired 'use' of the drug does not alter hereditary material.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Write Darwin's steps in order: variation → overproduction → struggle → survival of the fittest → inheritance. 'The giraffe stretched its neck so its children had long necks' is Lamarck and scores zero on a Darwin question. Weismann's mice are the standard reason Lamarck was rejected — mention tails.

points: Lamarck proposed use and disuse plus inheritance of acquired characters; Weismann's tailless mice showed acquired characters are not inherited.
Darwin's natural selection: inherited variation, overproduction, struggle, survival of those best suited, and passing on of their alleles.
The environment selects; the organism does not strive to evolve.
Peppered moths, antibiotic-resistant bacteria and the sickle-cell allele in malarial regions are applications of the same theory.
'Fittest' means best adapted to current conditions, not simply strongest or largest.
